proposal.intervention: Fabricate and characterize matched Au, Ag, and Ag-capped-Au substrates over a prespecified cap-thickness and morphology range. Adsorb the same molecular system using blocked, randomized preparations while measuring coverage, orientation, adsorption geometry, and chemical state independently. proposal.known_physics_envelope: Standard Raman and electromagnetic descriptions allow a measured band intensity to depend on Raman-tensor projection, local incident and scattered polarization, molecular position and orientation, excitation-frequency and Stokes-frequency local-field factors, chemical or adsorption state, detection response, and spatial sampling. A common multiplicative enhancement factor cancels from a ratio, but mode- or frequency-dependent transfer functions generally do not. Consequently, wavelength, cap thickness, morphology, and hot-spot sampling can change relative ratios within known physics. These effects may be nonmonotonic near resonances, can covary with coverage and chemistry, and do not imply a sharp phase transition, monotonic residual increase, or unique universal threshold.
proposal.local_falsifier: The conditional prediction is weakened if the orientation-only model remains calibrated on independent preparations after covariance validation, or if any apparent S association disappears after accounting for measured chemical state, adsorption state, and condition-dependent cross-band, spatial, preparation, and temporal covariance.
proposal.mechanistic_hypothesis: Within the tested conditions, relative Raman band ratios may depart from an orientation-and-adsorption-only prediction when band-specific excitation and Stokes-frequency transfer factors, local polarization, and molecularly weighted spatial sampling contribute an uncertainty-resolved effect comparable to the Raman-tensor projection effect. The expected relationship is a conditional crossover that may be nonmonotonic near resonances and may differ among Au, Ag, and Ag-capped-Au structures; it is not a claim of a singular physical boundary or new mechanism.
proposal.observable: For every sample, wavelength, polarization, and spatial region, measure the relative Raman band-ratio vector with calibrated uncertainty; independently measured orientation and adsorption-geometry distributions; coverage and chemical-state indicators; total enhancement; excitation- and Stokes-frequency transfer-function estimates; local polarization; molecularly weighted spatial heterogeneity; nuisance variables such as temperature and dose; and out-of-sample predictions and residuals from the orientation-only and broader known-physics models.

assumptions: Over each preregistered analysis interval, adsorption and exchange can be approximated by a stationary or locally stationary finite-state process, while allowing explicit tests for nonstationarity.

State occupancies, transition rates or residence-time distributions, orientation-sensitive observables, state-dependent spectra, and relevant field proxies can be measured independently or cross-validated sufficiently to constrain—not necessarily uniquely identify—the observation model.

The selected intervention changes exchange kinetics within a characterized range without an unmeasured compensating change in substrate morphology, analyte amount, chemical enhancement, charge transfer, photochemistry, local heating, or illumination history; residual changes are modeled rather than assumed absent.
Detector response, photon-counting noise, spectral bleed-through, drift, blinking, photobleaching, and exposure-induced perturbations are measured with controls and included in the observation model.
The approximately uniform-field comparison is operationally defined by an independently calibrated lower dispersion of the relevant field proxy, not inferred from the SERS data being tested.
State-resolved emission vectors can be estimated independently enough to test proportionality.
The ratio interaction is interpreted only when nonproportional spectral directions are supported.
controls: Use Au and Ag samples, or geometrically matched nanostructures, only after independently characterizing morphology, roughness, optical response, analyte loading, and thermal response; compare field-heterogeneity strata rather than treating material identity as the causal variable.

Measure orientation and adsorption occupancy with independent polarization, vibrational, fluorescence, or surface-sensitive observables; measure state-specific spectra and intensity distributions rather than relying on pooled SERS ratios to define the states.

Use stable spectral references, dark and blank controls, repeated substrates, randomized measurement order, interleaved low-power measurements, and intensity-dependent controls to quantify drift, contamination, photobleaching, charge transfer, and local heating.

Acquire band-vector trajectories at several preregistered integration windows spanning both shorter and longer than the independently estimated correlation time, with detector timing and photon-count statistics calibrated separately.

Include known-physics nuisance models for static orientation/access, adsorption exchange, spectral diffusion or blinking, chemical-enhancement fluctuations, photochemistry, and instrumental drift; compare their posterior-predictive performance rather than testing only an orientation-only null.

Analyze total-intensity covariance and ratio dispersion as separate preregistered outcomes.
proposal.development_value: This revision is a known-physics measurement and model-development proposal, not a claim of novel physics. It replaces the unsupported implication that changing residence time must change the mean band ratio with a testable prediction about temporal covariance, window dependence, and ratio-distribution bias. It also makes the broad null explicit: observed rate dependence can arise from ordinary adsorption kinetics, photophysics, chemical enhancement, or instrument effects and is not by itself evidence for residence-time-mediated electromagnetic sampling. The useful outcome is a calibrated protocol for determining which time-resolved SERS statistics are predictable from independently measured kinetics and observation physics.
proposal.heldout_test: Train models only on prespecified training windows and compare held-out predictions for total-intensity covariance, cross-band covariance, variance versus integration time, and ratio distributions. Require state-resolved emission vectors to be independently measured and nonproportional before treating ratio-dispersion changes as a kinetic prediction; if the vectors are proportional, evaluate covariance and ratio statistics as separate estimands. Report equivalent predictive performance as unresolved mechanism identification.

proposal.intervention: Use a within-sample, randomized intervention that changes adsorption exchange or residence kinetics while monitoring morphology and optical response before and after the intervention. Candidate interventions include a controlled temperature or solvent perturbation, a concentration-jump recovery, or a characterized ligand/surface-chemistry change; retain only perturbations for which independent kinetics, analyte loading, thermal state, and optical response are measured. Match or statistically adjust occupancy and average orientation, and measure rather than assume that state-specific emission and chemical-enhancement factors remain fixed. Compare the resulting temporal statistics across independently defined high- and low-field-heterogeneity samples, while holding acquisition settings fixed and repeating the intervention in both directions when feasible.
proposal.known_physics_envelope: The proposal is restricted to established Raman/SERS, adsorption-kinetic, photophysical, and measurement physics: linear or calibrated nonlinear spectral accumulation, electromagnetic enhancement, chemical enhancement and charge transfer, adsorption/desorption and site exchange, molecular reorientation, blinking or spectral diffusion, photobleaching, local heating, concentration fluctuations, detector response, photon-counting noise, and instrumental drift. For a stationary two-state continuous-time Markov component with rates alpha and beta, stationary occupancy is beta/(alpha+beta), the correlation time is 1/(alpha+beta), and the variance of a time average follows the integrated-exponential covariance expression. Scaling both rates by a common factor while preserving state emissions and stationary occupancy changes temporal covariance and finite-window ratio distributions but leaves the stationary pooled mean intensity ratio unchanged. Heterogeneous fields can alter the mapping from hidden-state trajectories to band vectors, but a larger rate effect in that regime is a conditional model prediction, not a general law. Deviations may reflect nonstationarity, chemical enhancement, photochemistry, blinking, heating, morphology changes, or model misspecification; they do not establish new physics.
proposal.local_falsifier: The ratio-dispersion component is locally falsified if independently measured proportional state-emission vectors predict invariant noiseless band ratios while observed dispersion is explained by calibrated noise, fitting error, drift, or other nuisance terms. The broader kinetic model is locally falsified if its independently parameterized held-out covariance and window-dependence predictions fail against a preregistered alternative. A residual covariance effect without nonproportional state spectra does not establish a ratio interaction.
proposal.mechanistic_hypothesis: A molecule's observed SERS band vector may be a time-weighted result of visits to adsorption environments with different orientations, emission responses, and electromagnetic enhancement. When exchange or residence times are comparable to the acquisition window or molecular reorientation time, this can produce rate-dependent autocovariance, cross-band covariance, and finite-window ratio distributions even when stationary occupancy and mean orientation are matched. The effect is expected to depend on field heterogeneity only through the specified observation model and must be distinguished from established dynamic adsorption, blinking, chemical-enhancement, photochemical, thermal, and instrumental processes.
proposal.observable: For each acquisition window, record the calibrated vector of integrated Raman band intensities and polarization-resolved channels. Derive temporal autocovariance and cross-band covariance, variance as a function of integration time, inter-window dependence, and the distribution of per-window ratios with uncertainty propagated from photon counting and spectral fitting. The primary estimand is the out-of-sample change in these statistics under an independently measured kinetic perturbation, conditional on occupancy, orientation, state emission, field-heterogeneity proxy, illumination, and nuisance controls. The pooled mean ratio is a secondary observable and is not expected to change under pure stationary common-rate scaling.
proposal.quantitative_or_ordinal_prediction: Common scaling of transition rates predicts a shorter temporal correlation time and reduced time-averaged intensity covariance, but no intrinsic kinetic change in band-ratio dispersion when state-emission vectors are proportional. A rate-dependent ratio effect and any stronger heterogeneous-field interaction are conditional on independently verified nonproportional, field-dependent spectral directions. The stationary pooled mean ratio remains invariant under pure common-rate scaling.
